title: Fair coin, $10 against $100
hook: Every bet is a fair coin flip. Does that give you an even chance of ending on top?

knows: a fair game has zero average gain per bet
doesNotKnow: that a small bankroll against a big one is usually ruined even in a fair game
that the chance of taking everything equals your share of the money

misconception: In a fair game the chance of ending richer equals the chance of ending poorer, whatever the stakes.
objective: The learner can say that in a fair $1-bet game you win everything with probability your stake / total money (10/110 = 9.1%), so the poorer side is usually ruined.
keyState: $10 stake: 30 seeded games drawn (2 reached $110), then 300 more (24 of 330); then $50 stake (13 of 30).

claims.text: In a fair game of $1 bets where you hold $a and the house $b, you end up with all $(a + b) with probability a / (a + b).
claims.source: Classical gambler's ruin result for a symmetric random walk (Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, vol. 1, ch. 14); exact(stake) = stake / 110 in model.ts.

claims.text: With $10 against $100 your chance of taking all $110 is 10/110 = 9.1%; with $50 against $60 it is 45.5%.
On the stage, 2 of 30 games from $10 reached $110, and 24 of 330 after 300 more; from $50, 13 of 30.
claims.source: Game g at stake a uses mulberry32(4000 + 1000 a + g), untuned (first seeds tried). Over 60 other seed sets: $10 / 30 games averaged 2.4 wins (SD 1.4, range 0 to 6); $10 / 330 games 29.3 (SD 4.7, range 19 to 39); $50 / 30 games 13.6 (SD 2.3, range 9 to 18). Expected 2.7, 30 and 13.6.

claims.text: Each bet is a fair coin, so the average change in your money per bet is zero.
claims.source: +1 or -1 with probability 1/2 each has mean 0.

claims.text: The poorer side is usually ruined while the rare wins run long: most lines on the stage end at $0.
claims.source: Follows from claim 2: from $10, 90.9% of games end in ruin. The drawn lines are a seeded illustration (claim 3).

claims.text: The model says nothing about the odds in real casinos, which are not fair.
claims.source: Scope statement: the lesson uses a fair coin and unlimited play until one side is out of money.

claims.text: In a fair game your expected money stays at its starting amount; you end with $0 or $110, so 110 times the chance of taking it all equals the stake (a martingale argument): with $10 the chance is 10/110.
claims.source: Optional stopping for a fair random walk (Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, vol. 1, ch. XIV); same result as c1.

recall.question: Fair coin, $1 bets. You hold $5 and your friend holds $95. You play until one of you has everything. Your chance of ending with it all?
recall.why: In a fair game your chance is your share of the money: 5 / 100 = 5%. Most games end in your ruin even though every bet is fair.
